articles.intro: Look at the whole drinking occasion: what is in the glass, what you eat with it and what happens the following day. A smaller, repeatable change beats pretending the weekend does not count.
sections: The drink counts before the takeaway does

Alcohol contains energy, and mixers can add more. The number depends on the drink, strength and serving size. A pint, bottle and large home pour are not interchangeable. Check the label or a reliable unit-and-calorie calculator for what you actually drink; guessing from the colour of the liquid is not much of a system.
Count units separately from calories

UK low-risk guidance advises adults not to regularly exceed 14 units a week, spread over at least three days if drinking that amount. This is a health-risk limit, not a weight-loss allowance or a target to use up. Lower-calorie alcohol still contains alcohol. Alcohol-free drinks can be useful, but check their label if calories matter to your plan.
Make Friday easier without wrecking Saturday

Before going out, decide on a limit and an ordinary evening meal. Drink at your own pace rather than keeping up with rounds. Have a non-alcoholic option you actually like. For the morning after, keep an easy breakfast or lunch ready instead of relying on whatever gets delivered fastest. These are planning examples, not a promise that a particular drink or routine will produce weight loss.
Review the occasion, not your character
Write down the drink and its real serving size, including home top-ups.
Notice food before, during and after the occasion without turning it into punishment.
Choose one change for next time: fewer rounds, a smaller measure, or a drink-free occasion.
Check whether that change helped your sleep, appetite or next-day plans.
When cutting down needs medical support

If delaying a drink brings shaking, sweating or other withdrawal symptoms, get medical advice before suddenly stopping or cutting down sharply. Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous. Speak to your GP or an alcohol support service if controlling drinking is difficult; a calorie tracker is not treatment for dependence. Severe withdrawal symptoms, including seizures or hallucinations, need emergency help.
Your next drinking occasion

Choose the one change you can put in place before the first drink. If a strict rule repeatedly falls apart, make the plan smaller and consider the support you need rather than doubling the punishment.
next: Find support in Good to Talk

articles.intro: Calories describe energy. They can help you understand portions and patterns, but a calculator cannot tell you exactly what your body will need every day.
sections: What the number means

Food labels usually show energy in kilocalories, written as kcal, and sometimes kilojoules, written as kJ. Your body uses energy for basic functions as well as movement. Body weight can change when intake and use differ over time. That does not make one high-calorie meal a failure or turn a daily estimate into a precise measurement.
A population average is not your prescription

The NHS gives 2,500 kcal a day as a guide for an average man, while explaining that needs vary with age, body size and activity. It is not a universal weight-loss target. Our calorie calculator is an estimate to discuss and adjust, not permission for a crash diet. Medical conditions, treatment and unusual nutritional needs may require individual advice.
Read the serving size before the big number

Compare the per-100g figure with the portion you actually eat. A packet described as two servings does not become one serving because you opened it alone. Include drinks, cooking oil, dressings and extras if you are tracking. For homemade meals, a reasonable estimate is often more useful than spending half the evening chasing a number you still cannot make exact.
Use the information to improve an ordinary meal

Keep the food you enjoy and look for a manageable adjustment: a measured amount of oil, vegetables alongside the main meal, or a portion of leftovers put away before sitting down. Choose one change and see whether the meal still satisfies you. The aim is a meal you can repeat, rather than the lowest number you can tolerate.
Tracking is optional, adequate nutrition is not

If counting makes you anxious, restrictive or preoccupied with food, stop treating the app as the boss. Regular meals and practical portion changes are alternatives to discuss with a dietitian or clinician. Do not compensate for eating by skipping needed food or forcing exercise. People with an eating-disorder history should seek suitable professional support before starting weight-loss tracking.
A useful check after a couple of weeks
Could I follow the approach on busy days?
Was I adequately fed and able to function?
Did my tracking include the things I usually forget?
Do I need a smaller change, more support or a different approach?

articles.intro: Build a habit around a real moment in your day, give it a smaller version for difficult weeks and review whether it helped. You do not need to rebuild your entire life by Monday.
sections: Choose a moment, not a vague intention

Eat better and move more describe a direction, not a plan. Try something you can recognise: make tomorrow's lunch while clearing dinner, walk a short familiar route after dropping the children off, or put a drink beside the place you work. These are examples to adapt to your life, rather than a scientifically guaranteed formula.
Remove the bit that keeps tripping you up

If lunch disappears because meetings overrun, keep an ordinary backup meal available. If your walking shoes are buried in the garage, leave them near the door. If an elaborate recipe never happens, use a simpler meal. A plan that requires a quieter job, different family and better weather probably needs editing.
Give the habit a minimum version

Write down what counts on a rough day. Your full plan might be preparing tomorrow's lunch; the minimum might be choosing a sandwich and fruit before leaving home. A longer walk might become a short comfortable outing. A smaller version keeps the choice available without pretending that every version delivers identical health benefits.
Do not promise yourself a magic deadline

There is no single number of days after which every habit becomes automatic. A missed day is information about the plan, not proof you cannot change. Restart at the next useful opportunity. Avoid making up for a missed task with extra restriction or a punishing workout.
Ask whether it helped, then change the right thing
If it did not fit the week, change the time, place or size.
If it was manageable but unhelpful, try a different action rather than insisting on more of it.
If it helped, keep it steady before adding another task.
If symptoms, pain or distress are getting in the way, seek appropriate advice rather than blaming the habit.
Make next week slightly easier

Pick one recurring snag and one response. Keep both short enough to remember. General food and activity advice can support health, but a habit checklist cannot diagnose a condition or replace prescribed treatment.
next: Keep your next step in My Timber

articles.intro: Forty is not a switch that makes weight management impossible. Start with what has changed in your actual week, then build food, movement and support around the life you have now.
sections: Compare routines before blaming your age

Look at an ordinary working day now and an ordinary day ten years ago. Are you sitting more, sleeping differently, drinking more often or eating later? Has an injury changed how you move? That comparison can reveal a practical starting point. It cannot diagnose why your weight changed, and it is not proof that hormones are the cause.
Keep dinner recognisable

Choose two or three meals you enjoy and can prepare on a busy day. Include a protein-containing food, vegetables or fruit where appropriate, and a starchy component in a portion that works for you. Beans, eggs, fish and other ordinary foods can do the job; a cupboard full of powders is not compulsory. Use the Eatwell Guide as an overall pattern, rather than demanding a perfect plate at every meal.
Build movement from your current starting point

Adults aged 19 to 64 are advised to work towards 150 minutes of moderate activity a week and strengthening activities on at least two days. Those are general goals, not instructions to go from the sofa to a punishing circuit tomorrow. Start within your ability. Get advice if an injury, medical condition or long period of inactivity affects what is appropriate.
Check health changes properly

Persistent fatigue, loud snoring with breathing pauses, sexual symptoms or unexplained weight change deserve a clinical conversation. Do not diagnose low testosterone from a quiz or buy treatment because an advert lists familiar symptoms. A home measurement or private test also needs a clear explanation of what happens if the result is abnormal.
An example first week
Choose one reliable lunch and have its ingredients available.
Add a short, comfortable movement slot on days it fits.
Notice whether a regular drinking occasion is making the next day harder.
Record one problem to discuss with your GP if symptoms are persistent.
At the end of the week, keep what helped and change what did not.
Use more than the scale

Notice whether everyday tasks feel easier, meals are less chaotic or your routine is more dependable. Weight trends can be useful, but treatment suitability and medicine changes belong with the clinician responsible for your care. You can work on everyday routines while seeking that support.
sources: NHS: sleep apnoea symptoms and assessment

articles.intro: A difficult night can make the next day's food and movement plans harder. Work on the routine you can change, and get persistent sleep problems or breathing pauses assessed properly.
sections: Separate a bad night from a persistent problem

Think about the pattern: trouble getting to sleep, frequent waking, a schedule that leaves too little time, or feeling exhausted despite enough opportunity to rest. Write down what happens and how it affects the day. That gives a clinician more to work with than simply saying you are tired. An app cannot determine the cause.
Make the next day easier to feed

After a poor night, reduce the number of decisions. Keep an ordinary breakfast or lunch available and decide dinner before you are hungry and worn out. A simple meal is a perfectly respectable response. Do not use fatigue as a reason for an extreme food restriction or an exercise session you cannot safely manage.
Try a repeatable evening routine

Choose a reasonably consistent bedtime and waking time where work allows. Give yourself a quieter wind-down period; notice whether late caffeine, alcohol or phone use makes sleep harder. Change one thing at a time so you can tell what helps. Shift work and caring responsibilities need a realistic plan, not advice written for somebody with an empty diary.
Snoring with breathing pauses needs attention

Breathing that stops and starts, gasping or choking noises during sleep and marked daytime tiredness are reasons to see a GP about possible sleep apnoea. Someone who has witnessed the symptoms can help explain them. Losing weight does not establish that sleep apnoea has resolved; keep using prescribed treatment until your sleep team advises otherwise.
Protect safety while you seek help

Do not drive or operate machinery when sleepiness makes it unsafe. If sleep apnoea is suspected or diagnosed, ask about treatment and the relevant driving rules. Persistent insomnia or sleep problems affecting daily life also deserve professional help. Buying another tracker is not a substitute for assessment.
A useful record for the appointment
When you go to bed, wake and work shifts.
How often you wake and whether someone notices breathing pauses.
Daytime sleepiness and its effect on work or driving.
Medicines, caffeine and alcohol that may be relevant.
What you have tried and whether it changed anything.
sources: NHS Every Mind Matters: sleep problems

articles.intro: Find the moment stress changes your eating or drinking, then make that moment easier. Food planning can help with the day; persistent distress deserves support of its own.
sections: Look for your actual pattern

Stress does not produce the same eating pattern in everyone. You may skip meals when busy, graze after work, or reach for alcohol when the house finally goes quiet. For a few days, note the situation and what you needed at the time. You do not have to count every calorie to notice that lunch keeps disappearing.
Prepare for the difficult hour

If you usually arrive home ravenous, have something straightforward ready: leftovers, a sandwich, eggs on toast or another meal that suits your needs. Decide before the stressful moment. A planned meal cannot remove the pressure at work, but it can stop dinner becoming one more problem to solve.
Give yourself another way to come down

Try a short comfortable walk, a call to someone you trust, a quiet few minutes or an activity you enjoy. Choose something accessible rather than another performance target. Movement can help with how stress feels, but it does not magically fix debt, caring pressures, conflict or an unsafe workplace. The cause may need practical help as well.
Avoid the compensation cycle

Eating more than planned does not require skipping the next meal or exercising as punishment. Return to your ordinary routine. If eating feels out of control, or guilt and restriction are becoming a pattern, ask a GP or appropriate professional for help. A stricter calorie limit is not the answer to every difficulty.
Know when everyday advice is not enough

Seek support if stress persists, affects sleep or functioning, or is leading to harmful drinking or other behaviours. If you have withdrawal symptoms when delaying alcohol, get medical advice before stopping suddenly. Good to Talk can help you find a starting point, but My Timber is not a crisis service or a substitute for mental-health care.
One thing to change this week
Name the difficult moment: for example, getting home after a late shift.
Choose one food backup and one way to decompress.
Tell somebody if you need practical support.
Review whether the response helped; change the approach if it did not.
sources: NHS: practical ways to reduce stress

articles.intro: Walking is useful because you can fit it around ordinary life. Start with a route you can repeat comfortably, build gradually and judge progress by more than a step counter.
sections: Walking counts, but it is not a weight-loss guarantee

Walking adds activity and can support fitness and health. The effect on weight varies with the wider picture, including food, health and what you can sustain. A watch's calorie estimate is not a precise allowance to eat back, and 10,000 steps is not a compulsory starting line.
Choose a repeatable first route

If you are able to walk, start with a short familiar route and a pace comfortable for you. Consider the surface, hills, lighting and a place to rest if needed. Supportive, comfortable footwear matters more than buying specialist kit for a short local walk. Increase distance gradually rather than turning the first outing into a test.
Understand brisk without chasing a stranger's speed

Moderate-intensity activity raises breathing and heart rate; the NHS suggests that being able to talk but not sing is a useful guide. Brisk walking can count towards the adult weekly activity goal. If you are rebuilding activity after a long break, your appropriate pace may be slower. There is no prize for matching somebody else's fitness.
An example that fits a working week

Choose three convenient opportunities, such as after lunch, part of the journey home or while waiting for a children's activity. Have a shorter route for days when time disappears. Record whether it fitted and how you felt afterwards. When the routine feels manageable, add a little time or another opportunity. This is an example to adapt, not a rehabilitation prescription.
Adapt rather than push through pain

Joint problems may require shorter outings, another type of movement or advice from a clinician or physiotherapist. Stop if activity brings concerning symptoms such as chest pain, faintness or unusual severe breathlessness and seek appropriate medical help. Get advice before starting if health concerns or prolonged inactivity make your safe level uncertain.
What to keep track of
How often you got out and whether the route fitted your day.
Comfort during the walk and recovery afterwards.
Whether everyday tasks are becoming easier.
What needs changing: time, terrain, footwear, pace or support.
